claim: Researcher degrees of freedom in data collection and analysis can lead to fundamentally different results and conclusions despite identical raw data.
source: Importantly and concerningly, these different paths can lead to fundamentally different end-points (i.e., results and associated conclusions) despite an identical starting point (i.e., raw data) (Silberzahn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Silberzahn et al., 2018

claim: Researchers often take certain analytical paths without malicious intent to obtain favorable results.
source: Often, researchers take a certain path without malicious intent to obtain favorable results (e.g., 'p-hacking'; Head et al., 2015): the decision to follow a certain path may be based on unawareness of alternative paths (due to lack of specific background knowledge) or the researcher following the most obvious path from an individual perspective.
evidence: Supported by citation to Head et al., 2015 and logical reasoning about researcher behavior

claim: Fear conditioning is a paradigm employed to study emotional learning and memory processes with a strong translational perspective.
source: Fear conditioning is a typical paradigm employed to study (emotional) learning and memory processes with a particularly strong translational perspective (Lonsdorf et al., 2017; Vervliet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lonsdorf et al., 2017 and Vervliet et al., 2013

claim: Participants are often excluded from fear conditioning analyses if they appear to not have learned or not have been responsive during fear acquisition training.
source: Therefore, participants are often (routinely) excluded from analyses if they appear to not have learned ('non-learners') or not have been responsive to the experimental stimuli ('non-responders') during fear acquisition training, in which one conditional stimulus (CS+) predicts an upcoming aversive unconditioned stimulus (US) and another conditional stimulus does not (CS–) (Lonsdorf et al., 2017; Pavlov, 1927).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lonsdorf et al., 2017 and Pavlov, 1927

claim: Non-learning is most often defined as a failure to show discrimination between CS+ and CS- in skin conductance responses.
source: Critically, 'non-learning' is most often defined as a failure to show discrimination between the CS+ and CS– in skin conductance responses (SCRs) – the most common outcome measure in the field (Lonsdorf et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lonsdorf et al., 2017

claim: SCRs are not a pure measure of learning or fear, but rather reflect arousal levels that serve as proxies for fear learning.
source: As SCRs are not a pure measure of either learning or fear, but rather reflect arousal levels (Hamm et al., 1993) that serve as proxies for fear learning, classification into 'learners' and 'non-learners' on the basis of this single outcome measure may induce substantial sample bias.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamm et al., 1993 and logical inference about sample bias

claim: Defining non-learning on a single outcome measure like SCRs ignores that successful CS+/CS- differentiation may be present in other outcome measures.
source: First, defining 'non-learning' on one single outcome measure, such as SCRs, ignores the fact that successful CS+/CS– differentiation may be present in other outcome measures (Hamm et al., 1993) such as fear potentiated startle (FPS) or ratings of fear and contingencies (i.e., cognitive awareness of the CS+/US contingencies).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamm et al., 1993

claim: The level of responding in SCRs and CS+/CS- discrimination is associated with numerous individual difference factors including age, sex, ethnicity, genetic makeup, use of oral contraceptives, and personality traits.
source: Second, the level of responding in SCRs and CS+/CS– discrimination has been shown to be associated with a vast number of individual difference factors (Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017; Boucsein et al., 2012) such as age and sex (for a discussion see Boucsein et al., 2012), ethnicity (Alexandra Kredlow et al., 2017; Boucsein et al., 2012), genetic make-up (Garpenstrand et al., 2001), use of oral contraceptives (Merz et al., 2018b) or personality traits (Naveteur and Freixa I Baque, 1987).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies

claim: Excluding participants as non-learners may pre-select specific sub-samples and hamper the generalizability and interpretation of findings.
source: Consequently, excluding participants from an experiment as 'non-learners' may pre-select specific sub-samples and thus may thus severely hamper the generalizability and interpretation of the findings.
evidence: Logical inference based on the association between SCR discrimination and individual differences

claim: Patients suffering from anxiety disorders show overgeneralization of fear responding, which is enhanced when responding to the CS-.
source: In fact, a recent meta-analysis suggests that patients suffering from anxiety disorders show overgeneralization of fear responding, which is enhanced when responding to the CS– (Duits et al., 2015), which may lead to reduced CS+/CS– discrimination if the response to the CS+ is comparable.
evidence: Supported by citation to meta-analysis by Duits et al., 2015

claim: Slightly fewer than one fourth (22%) of the records in the systematic literature search employed performance-based exclusion of participants.
source: Slightly fewer than one fourth of the records (i.e., 22%; 11 out of 50 records comprising 14 individual studies as three records reported two studies each) included in the systematic literature search employed performance-based exclusion of participants (i.e., SCR 'non-learners', Figure 1).
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 1

claim: Every single record that employed performance-based exclusion used an idiosyncratic definition to define non-learners, yielding a total of eleven different definitions in six months.
source: Strikingly, every single one of these records used an idiosyncratic definition to define 'non-learners', yielding a total of eleven different definitions in the short period of six months (see Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Based on data extraction from systematic literature search

claim: The percentages of excluded participants varied from 2% to 74% of the respective study sample.
source: The percentages of excluded participants varied from 2% to 74% (Figure 2A) of the respective study sample.
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 2A

claim: The proportion of participants excluded is higher when CS+/CS- discrimination is calculated on the basis of raw data rather than log-transformed and range-corrected data.
source: Strikingly, the proportion of participants that are excluded is higher when CS+/CS– discrimination is calculated on the basis of raw data rather than log-transformed and range-corrected data (despite employing the same criteria) in particular for the highest 'non-learner' <0.01 µS cutoff (76.7% versus 52.6%, respectively) (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 1 as shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: High CS+/CS- discrimination cutoffs favor individuals with high SCR amplitudes to remain in the final sub-sample.
source: These two case examples illustrate that high CS+/CS– discrimination cutoffs favor individuals with high SCR amplitudes to remain in the final sub-sample.
evidence: Based on case examples illustrated in Figure 3A showing two individuals with same discrimination ratio but different amplitudes

claim: The exclusion group defined by a CS+/CS- discrimination cutoff <0 µS showed inverse discrimination (CS->CS+) that was not significant in raw SCRs but significant in log,rc SCRs.
source: Unsurprisingly, the exclusion group defined by a CS+/CS– discrimination cutoff <0 µS showed inverse discrimination (CS–>CS+, not significant in raw SCRs [p=0.117]; significant in log,rc SCRs [p = 0.021]).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of Data set 1

claim: Most cumulative exclusion groups established by defining non-learners by CS+/CS- discrimination cutoffs in SCRs show statistically significant CS+/CS- discrimination.
source: Strikingly and more importantly, most cumulative exclusion groups, as established by defining 'non-learners' by the CS+/CS– discrimination different cutoffs in SCRs in the literature, in fact show statistically significant CS+/CS– discrimination (see Appendix 2 for details and a brief discussion).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of Data set 1 as detailed in Appendix 2

claim: Individuals with non-significant and inverse CS+/CS- discrimination in SCRs showed significant CS+/CS- discrimination in fear ratings.
source: In fact, individuals with non-significant and inverse CS+/CS– discrimination (i.e., ≤0 µS) in SCRs showed significant CS+/CS– discrimination in fear ratings (t31 = 9.69, pbonf_corr < 0.000000001, d = 1.71, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of Data set 1 as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: All cumulative exclusion groups showed significant CS+/CS- discrimination in fear ratings.
source: Importantly, all cumulative exclusion groups showed significant CS+/CS– discrimination in fear ratings (all p 's< 0.002, see Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of Data set 1 as detailed in Appendix 3—table 1

claim: The classification as learners and non-learners changes if two features (CS+/CS- discrimination cutoff and full vs. last half of acquisition training phase) of the criteria are changed.
source: We also illustrate (Figure 4) that the classification as 'learners' and 'non-learners' changes if two features (CS+/CS- discrimination cutoff and full vs. last half of acquisition training phase) of the criteria are changed (as illustrated in their full variation in Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on analysis of Data set 1 as shown in Figure 4

claim: The distributions of trait anxiety were shifted to the left (towards lower scores) with higher SCR CS+/CS- discrimination cutoffs.
source: Regarding the impact of performance-based exclusion on the pre-selection for certain individual differences, Figure 5 shows that the distributions of trait anxiety were shifted to the left (i.e., towards lower scores) with higher SCR CS+/CS– discrimination cutoffs.
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 2 as shown in Figure 5

claim: Highly anxious individuals display smaller CS+/CS- discrimination in SCRs.
source: More precisely, this means that, in this sample, highly anxious individuals display smaller CS+/CS– discrimination in SCRs, and that excluding individuals who display low discrimination scores will lead to the exclusion of anxious individuals.
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 2 showing association between trait anxiety and discrimination

claim: A main effect of Exclusion group on trait anxiety score was observed (F[4,263] = 219.2, p<0.001, ƞP2 = 0.77).
source: In fact, we observed a main effect of 'Exclusion group' on trait anxiety score (F[4,263] = 219.2, p<0.001, ƞP2 = 0.77).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of Data set 2

claim: All exclusion groups differ significantly from each other in their trait anxiety scores except for specific comparisons.
source: All exclusion groups (corresponding to the color coding in Figure 5) differ significantly from each other in their trait anxiety scores (all pbonf_corr ≤ 0.001), except for the group that did not show any CS+/CS– discrimination (=0 µS, light green, however n = 6 only), which showed significantly higher trait anxiety scores (mean ± SD STAI score: 43.8 ± 6.1) than the group with the largest CS+/CS– discrimination only (i.e., ≥0.1 µS, dark blue, n = 88, mean ± SD STAI score: 36.6 ± 8.5, pbonf_corr ≤ 0.001, CI [0.133 to 0.279]).
evidence: Based on post-hoc statistical analysis of Data set 2

claim: Thirty-two percent of the records in the systematic literature search included a definition and exclusion of non-responders.
source: Thirty-two percent (i.e., 16 records) of the records in our systematic literature search included a definition and exclusion of 'non-responders', with percentages of participants excluded as a result of non-responding ranging between 0% and 14% (see Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 6A

claim: The definitions of non-responders differed in stimulus type(s) used, SCR minimum amplitude criterion, and percentage of trials for which criteria have to be met.
source: The definitions differed in: i) the stimulus type(s) used to define 'non-responding' (CS+ reinforced, CS+ unreinforced, all CS+s, CS–, US), ii) the SCR minimum amplitude criterion used to define a responder (varying between 0.01 µS and 0.05 µS; visual inspection), and iii) the percentage of trials for which these criteria have to be met (see Figure 6B and Appendix 1—table 2), as well as a combination thereof.
evidence: Based on data extraction from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 6B and Appendix 1—table 2

claim: Non-responding was most commonly defined as not showing a sufficient number of responses to the conditioned stimuli (CS+ and/or CS-).
source: 'Non-responding' was most commonly defined as not showing a sufficient number of responses to the conditioned stimuli (CS+ and CS–), less frequently by the absence of responses to the US or any stimulus (CS+, CS- or US), and in two cases by the absence of responses to the CS+ or context (CXT+) specifically (see Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 6B

claim: The percentage of excluded participants differed substantially depending on the stimulus type used to define non-responding.
source: Not surprisingly, the percentage of excluded participants differed substantially depending on the stimulus type used to define 'non-responding' (CS based, 0–10%; CS+/CXT+ based, 10–11%; US based, 0–4%; CS and US based, 11–14%; pre-experimental test based, 5%; Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 6A

claim: The number of non-responses to the US was low (10% in Data set 1), while the number of non-responses to the CS was substantially higher (48.29%).
source: As expected from Figure 6A, the number of 'non-responses' to the US was low (as was also the case in our data [10%, Data set 1]), while the number of 'non-responses' to the CS (48.29%) was substantially higher – in particular for the CS– (58.6%; CS+ 'non-responses': 37.9%, see Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on analysis of Data set 1 as shown in Figure 7A

claim: All individuals that did not react to the US in more than two thirds of the US trials also showed no responses to the CS.
source: Furthermore, in our data (Data set 1), all individuals that did not react to the US in more than two thirds of the US trials also showed no responses to the CS (n = 3 of N = 119).
evidence: Based on analysis of Data set 1

claim: Non-responding to the US may predict non-responding to the CS but not vice versa.
source: To summarize, this provides the first evidence that 'non-responding' to the US may predict 'non-responding' to the CS but not vice versa.
evidence: Based on inference from analysis of Data set 1

claim: There is a positive correlation between the number of non-responses to the US and the number of non-responses to the CS.
source: Furthermore, our data also suggest a positive correlation between the number of 'non-responses' to the US and the number of 'non-responses' to the CS (see Figure 7B for statistics).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of Data set 1 as shown in Figure 7B

claim: Participant exclusion in fear conditioning research is common (40% of records included) and characterized by substantial operationalizational heterogeneity.
source: In this article, we showed that participant exclusion in fear conditioning research is common (i.e., 40% of records included) and characterized by substantial operationalizational heterogeneity of definitions for 'non-learners' and (physiological) 'non-responders'.
evidence: Based on results from systematic literature search

claim: Some definitions of non-learners are futile when those classified as non-learners in fact show significant discrimination on both ratings and SCRs.
source: Furthermore, we provide case-examples that illustrate: i) the futility of some definitions of 'non-learners' (i.e., when those classified as 'non-learners' in fact show significant discrimination on both ratings and SCRs as illustrated in Appendix 3 and Appendix 2, respectively) when applied to our data
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 1 as detailed in Appendices 2 and 3

claim: Excluding non-learners introduces potential sample bias with respect to individual differences.
source: and ii) the potential sample bias induced by excluding 'non-learners' with respect to individual differences.
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 2 showing association with trait anxiety

claim: Every single record in the systematic literature search that employed definitions of non-learners used a set of idiosyncratic criteria.
source: Operationalizational heterogeneity is illustrated by every single record in our systematic literature search (covering a six months period) that employed definitions of 'non-learners' using a set of idiosyncratic criteria.
evidence: Based on data extraction from systematic literature search

claim: In the records included, 6-52% of participants were excluded (disregarding one study reporting 74%).
source: In the records included here, 6–52% of participants were excluded (disregarding one study reporting percentages of 'non-learners' and 'non-responders' together with 74%; cf. Figure 2A), which substantially exceed the percentages recently put forward for 'non-learning' exclusions (Marin et al., 2019) that were suggested to lie between 4% (Chauret et al., 2014) and 19% (Oyarzún et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Figure 2A, with comparison to published estimates

claim: If several thousand analytical pipelines can be applied, the likelihood of false positives is high.
source: If several thousand analytical pipelines can be applied, the likelihood of false positives is high (Munafò et al., 2017) and the temptation of their opportunistic (ab)use must be considered a threat.
evidence: Supported by citation to Munafò et al., 2017

claim: Performance-based exclusion of participants is often based on a single outcome measure (typically SCRs), despite multiple measures being recorded.
source: First, 'performance-based exclusion of participants' is often based on a single outcome measure (typically SCRs), despite multiple measures being recorded (for exceptions see Ahmed and Lovibond, 2019; Belleau et al., 2018; Oyarzún et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on observation from systematic literature search with citations to exceptions

claim: Fear learning cannot be reliably inferred by means of SCRs because SCRs capture arousal-related processes and can only be used as a proxy to infer fear learning.
source: Importantly, 'fear learning' cannot be reliably inferred by means of SCRs, because SCRs capture arousal-related processes and can only be used as a proxy to infer 'fear learning' as fear is closely linked to arousal (Hamm and Weike, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hamm and Weike, 2005

claim: Physiological proxies of fear do not map onto fear itself.
source: Relatedly, the fact that physiological proxies of 'fear' do not map onto 'fear' itself has been discussed extensively (LeDoux, 2012; LeDoux, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to LeDoux, 2012 and LeDoux, 2014

claim: Individuals that fail to show CS+/CS- discrimination in SCRs may show substantial discrimination in other outcome measures such as ratings of fear, US expectancy or fear potentiated startle.
source: Second, but related, individuals that fail to show CS+/CS– discrimination in SCRs may show substantial discrimination, as an indicator of successful learning, in other outcome measures such as ratings of fear, US expectancy or fear potentiated startle (Hamm and Weike, 2005; Marin et al., 2019), as illustrated here for fear ratings (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Appendix 3—table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hamm and Weike, 2005 and Marin et al., 2019, and demonstrated in Data set 1

claim: There is some evidence that CS+/CS- discrimination during fear acquisition training does not necessarily predict CS+/CS- discrimination during other experimental phases.
source: To our knowledge, there is some evidence (Craske et al., 2008; Plendl and Wotjak, 2010; Prenoveau et al., 2013) that this theoretical assumption does not necessarily hold true, (i.e., CS+/CS– discrimination during fear acquisition training does not necessarily predict CS+/CS– discrimination during other experimental phases) (Gerlicher et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Craske et al., 2008; Plendl and Wotjak, 2010; Prenoveau et al., 2013; and Gerlicher et al., 2019

claim: Those classified as a group of non-learners in SCRs on the basis of identified definitions in fact displayed significant CS+/CS- discrimination when applied to the authors' own data, with an exception for cutoffs <0.05 µS.
source: Fourth, we provided empirical evidence that those classified as a group of 'non-learners' in SCRs in the literature (sometimes referred to as 'outliers') on the basis of the identified definitions in fact displayed significant CS+/CS– discrimination when applied to our own data. An exception to this was using cut offs in differential responding of <0.05 µS (note, however, that a non-significant CS+/CS– discrimination effect in the group of 'non-learners' as a whole cannot be taken as evidence that all individuals in this group do not in fact display meaningful or statistically significant CS+/CS– discrimination).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 1 as detailed in Appendix 2

claim: CS+/CS- discrimination in SCRs during fear acquisition training has been linked to a number of individual difference factors.
source: Fifth, we illustrate a concerning sample bias that is introduced by performance-based participant exclusion. CS+/CS– discrimination in SCRs during fear acquisition training has been linked to a number of individual difference factors (Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lonsdorf and Merz, 2017

claim: Selecting participants on the basis of SCR CS+/CS- discrimination will also select them on the basis of individual differences.
source: and, naturally, selecting participants on the basis of SCR CS+/CS– discrimination will also select them on the basis of these individual differences (illustrated by our case example on trait anxiety, Figure 5).
evidence: Logical inference illustrated by re-analysis of Data set 2 shown in Figure 5

claim: Excluding non-learners biases the sample towards low anxiety scores in the case example.
source: In our case example, we illustrate that excluding 'non-learners' biases the sample towards low anxiety scores, which hampers the generalizability and replicability of findings
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Data set 2 showing association between exclusion and trait anxiety

claim: High CS+/CS- discrimination cutoffs generally favor individuals with high SCR amplitudes despite potentially identical ratios between CS+ and CS- amplitudes.
source: Sixth, as illustrated by our case example (Figure 3), high CS+/CS– discrimination cutoffs generally favor individuals with high SCR amplitudes despite potentially identical ratios between CS+ and CS– amplitudes, which may introduce a sampling bias for individuals characterized by high arousal levels that probably have biological underpinnings.
evidence: Based on case examples illustrated in Figure 3

claim: Routinely excluding participants characterized by specific individual differences represents a major threat to generalizability, replicability and potentially clinical translation of findings.
source: Routinely, excluding participants who are intentionally or unintentionally characterized by specific individual differences represents a major threat to generalizability, replicability and potentially clinical translation of findings, as results might be contingent on a specific sub-sample and specific sample characteristics.
evidence: Logical inference based on the demonstrated sample bias

claim: The definition of non-responders, like that of non-learners, varies widely across studies.
source: We showed that the definition of 'non-responders', like that of 'non-learners', varies widely across studies.
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search

claim: Heterogeneity in definitions of non-responders manifests in different cutoff criteria, number of trials, and stimulus type(s) considered.
source: Heterogeneity in definitions manifests in different cutoff criteria for what is considered a valid response, the number of trials and the stimulus type(s) considered (Appendix 1—table 2, Figure 6).
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search as shown in Appendix 1—table 2 and Figure 6

claim: Most definitions of non-responders are based on CS responses and only few are based on US responses.
source: Surprisingly, most definitions are based on CS responses (i.e., SCRs to the CS+ and/or CS–) and only few are based on US responses.
evidence: Based on data from systematic literature search

claim: Non-responding to the CS is not necessarily indicative of physiological non-responding, especially if high cutoffs are used.
source: This highlights a potentially problematic overlap between 'non-learners' and 'non-responders': 'non-responding' to the CS (i.e., CS+ and CS– or CS+ only) is not necessarily indicative of physiological 'non-responding' – especially if high cutoffs are used.
evidence: Logical inference based on the distinction between learning-based and physiological responding

claim: Non-responding to the CS may reflect the absence of learning-based patterns in physiological responding, which may carry important information.
source: In fact, 'non-responding' to the CS may, or at least in some cases, reflect the absence of learning-based patterns in physiological responding – which may carry important information.
evidence: Logical inference about the meaning of CS non-responding

claim: Striking differences in percentages of non-responses to the US (10%) and CS (48%) were observed in Data set 1.
source: Having observed the striking differences in percentages of 'non-responses' to the US (10%) and CS (48%) observed in our data (see Figure 7 and Appendix 4—table 1), we suggest that physiological 'non-responding' cannot and should not be determined on the basis of the absence of responding to the CS.
evidence: Based on analysis of Data set 1 as shown in Figure 7 and Appendix 4—table 1

claim: Physiological non-responding cannot and should not be determined on the basis of the absence of responding to the CS.
source: we suggest that physiological 'non-responding' cannot and should not be determined on the basis of the absence of responding to the CS.
evidence: Inference based on the observed differences in non-response rates between US and CS

claim: The group of non-responders probably lumps together several sub-groups including those with technical problems, those who fell asleep or did not pay attention, those who learned cognitively but did not express expected SCR responses, and those who were attentive but did not learn the contingencies.
source: More globally, the group of 'non-responders', as defined by the criteria identified here, probably lumps together several sub-groups: individuals (1) for whom technical problems resulted in no valid SCRs, (2) who fell asleep or did not pay attention, (3) who cognitively learned the CS+/US contingencies but did not express the expected corresponding responses in SCRs, and (4) who were attentive to the experiment but did not learn the contingencies (i.e., unaware participants) and hence did not show the expected SCR patterns (Tabbert et al., 2011).
evidence: Logical inference with citation to Tabbert et al., 2011 for unaware participants

claim: Excluding physiological non-responders makes sense as a manipulation check independent of the hypothesis.
source: In summary, although excluding physiological 'non-responders' makes sense (in terms of a manipulation check and independent of the hypothesis), we consider defining 'non-responders' on the basis of the absence of SCRs to the CS as problematic (dependent on the hypothesis).
evidence: Authors' recommendation based on logical reasoning

claim: Physiological SCR non-responders should be defined on the basis of US responses during fear acquisition training or to strong stimuli during pre-conditioning phases.
source: We suggest that physiological SCR 'non-responders' should be defined on the basis of US responses during fear acquisition training or to strong stimuli during pre-conditioning phases such as US calibration, startle habituation or forced breathing (reliably eliciting strong SCRs).
evidence: Authors' recommendation based on empirical findings

claim: It is difficult to suggest a universally valid cutoff for the number or percentage of required valid US responses because this critically depends on variables such as hardware and sampling rate used.
source: If 'non-responding' to the US (during fear acquisition training) is used, it is difficult to suggest a universally valid cutoff with respect to the number or percentage of required valid US responses, because this critically depends on a number of variables such as hardware and sampling rate used.
evidence: Logical reasoning about factors affecting cutoff determination

claim: The cutoff for valid US responses may typically range between 1/3 and 2/3 of valid responses but may be data-set specific.
source: Appendix 4 suggests that the cutoff may typically range between 1/3 and 2/3 of valid responses but may be data-set specific.
evidence: Based on data presented in Appendix 4

claim: Transparency can be enhanced if authors report statistical results both with and without eliminated observations.
source: More precisely, transparency can be enhanced 'if observations are eliminated, authors must also report what the statistical results are if those observations are included', as suggested by Simmons and colleagues, nearly a decade ago (Simmons et al., 2011, Table 2).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to Simmons et al., 2011

claim: If a finding turns out to be contingent on the exclusion of non-learners, this does not necessarily invalidate the finding but may further specify it or hint to possible mechanisms and/or boundary conditions.
source: This being said, it is important to point out that should a finding turn out to be contingent on the exclusion of 'non-learners', this does not necessarily invalidate this finding. On the contrary, it may further specify the finding or hint to possible mechanisms and/or boundary conditions – yet inferences on boundary conditions should be made carefully (Hardwicke and Shanks, 2016).
evidence: Logical reasoning with citation to Hardwicke and Shanks, 2016

claim: Adopting an open science culture will facilitate transparent reporting of exclusion criteria and minimize the risk of exploiting heterogeneous definitions.
source: Relatedly, adopting an open science culture will facilitate transparent reporting of exclusion criteria (Nosek et al., 2015) and will minimize the risk of exploiting heterogeneous definitions in the field.
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to Nosek et al., 2015

claim: Registered reports, publicly available data, and pre-registration of definitions and analysis pipelines may be helpful.
source: Registered reports (Hardwicke and Ioannidis, 2018), publicly available data including those from excluded participants and pre-registration (Munafò et al., 2017) of definitions and analysis pipelines (Ioannidis, 2014), as well as openly accessible lab-specific standard operational protocols (SOPs), may also be helpful.
evidence: Recommendations supported by citations to Hardwicke and Ioannidis, 2018; Munafò et al., 2017; and Ioannidis, 2014

claim: The compilation of exclusion criteria employed in the records required extensive personal exchange with authors because the definitions provided were often insufficient, ambiguous or incorrect.
source: It was striking that the compilation of exclusion criteria ('non-learners' and 'non-responders', see Appendix 1—tables 1 and 2) employed in the records included in our systematic literature search required extensive personal exchange with the authors because the definitions provided were often insufficient, ambiguous or incorrect.
evidence: Based on authors' experience during data extraction from systematic literature search

claim: Graphical illustration of results should allow for complete presentation of data without obscuring important patterns, providing detailed distributional information rather than merely presenting summary statistics.
source: Our recommendations to improve the level of reporting details and transparency extends to the graphical illustration of results, which should optimally allow for a complete presentation of data (Weissgerber et al., 2015) without risking obscuring important patterns, providing detailed distributional information rather than merely presenting summary statistics (see Weissgerber et al., 2015 for a discussion).
evidence: Recommendation supported by citation to Weissgerber et al., 2015

claim: If criteria for non-learners or non-responders are employed, a sanity or manipulation check should be performed to determine whether non-learners really did not learn.
source: Finally, if criteria for 'non-learners' or 'non-responders' are employed to exclude participants from data analyses (or continuation of the experiment), we recommend that a sanity or manipulation check should be performed to determine whether – for instance - 'non-learners' really did not learn (i.e., really do not show significant CS+/CS– discrimination).
evidence: Authors' recommendation based on empirical findings

claim: Most definitions of non-learners fail the manipulation check that non-learners really did not learn.
source: We have empirically illustrated that most definitions of 'non-learners' fail this manipulation check (Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of Data set 1 as detailed in Appendix 2—table 1

claim: Authors should adequately justify all details of exclusion criteria both theoretically and practically.
source: Relatedly, we urge authors to justify adequately all details of the exclusion criteria (if applied) – both theoretically and practically.
evidence: Authors' recommendation

claim: It is neither ethical nor scientifically meaningful to exclude up to two thirds of a sample.
source: We argue that it is neither ethical (due to an excessive waste of tax money and human resources) nor scientifically meaningful to exclude up to two thirds of a sample.
evidence: Authors' argument based on ethical and scientific reasoning

claim: Findings derived from highly selective sub-samples may not generalize to other samples or to the general population and might be a threat to clinical translation.
source: We have shown that findings derived from such highly selective sub-samples may not generalize to other samples or to the general population, and as a consequence might be a threat to clinical translation.
evidence: Based on empirical findings from re-analyses showing sample bias

claim: Findings derived from highly selective samples have been routinely and invariantly generalized to reflect general principles and processes in the past.
source: Most problematically, however, findings derived from such highly selective samples have been routinely and invariantly generalized to reflect 'general principles' and 'processes' in the past.
evidence: Authors' observation about field practices

claim: Exclusions of non-learners can be dangerous if not handled transparently because they may bias and confuse a whole research field and may push research along a misleading path.
source: As such, exclusions of 'non-learners' can in fact be dangerous if not handled transparently (as suggested above), because they may bias and confuse a whole research field and may push research along a misleading path.
evidence: Authors' argument based on logical inference about consequences of non-transparent exclusions
